1.pericope_label: O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good: to him that by wisdom made the heavens

schools.summary: Augustine raises the difficulty that after the last judgment there will be none left miserable for God to pity, and answers that the blessedness mercifully bestowed on the miserable has itself no end, so that the mercy by which the unjust become just and the dead alive is everlasting in its effect.

Gill follows Aben Ezra and Kimchi in taking the gods for angels and reports a heathen title of the same shape, and makes the Lord of lords the Messiah; Calvin traces the artifice of the burden to the later period through a writer he quotes at length, defends the repetition by the practice of profane poets, and makes the plural titles a concession to the human tendency to divide the Godhead.

Henry gathers angels, magistrates and pretended deities into the plural titles, asks that thanks be given because God is good and not only because he does good, warns that the lights are called great because they appear so to us though astronomers know the moon is smaller than many stars, and observes that we are never so earnestly called upon to pray or repent as to give thanks; Spurgeon calls God the unrivalled Wonderworker and finds the microscope as full of wonders as the telescope.

Clarke takes the psalm for a responsive song of Levites and people written after the captivity by an unknown author, refuses to apply the plural titles to idols and applies them to priests and to magistrates, would render the burden as a tender mercy reserved for the coming age, and reads the stretching of the earth of a central abyss of waters not yet disproved; Wesley takes the gods for angels, princes or idols indifferently.

Keil and Delitzsch count the refrain as an intercalary verse repeated twenty-six times, report the disputed compass of the great Hallel, trace six-line strophes turning into eight-line ones from the point where dependence on the preceding psalm becomes borrowing, and note a printed Psalter that sets the psalm in two columns without manuscript warrant; Ellicott finds the creation section recalling the older account but borrowing its vocabulary elsewhere, so that the earth is a plate beaten out and spread on the waters rather than emerging from them.

debates: Who are the gods and lords of the opening verses? Gill follows Aben Ezra and Kimchi for angels and cites a heathen title of the same form; Clarke rules out idols on the ground that God is not their god and takes the titles of priests and of magistrates; Wesley admits angels, princes and idols alike; Henry takes all three at once; Calvin declines the question and makes the plural a concession to the human habit of dividing the Godhead into parts.

How does this creation account stand to the older one? Ellicott finds the section recalling it while drawing its words from a prophet, so that the earth is beaten out like metal and spread on the waters instead of emerging from them, and the word for lights means light rather than luminaries; Clarke reads the same clause of a central abyss of waters whose existence has not been disproved; Henry qualifies the greatness of the lights as an appearance, the moon being smaller than many stars but nearer.

When and how was the psalm made? Clarke finds no title in the Hebrew or any version, holds it written after the captivity by an unknown hand, and takes it for a responsive song with Levites and people alternating; Calvin quotes a writer who makes the burden characteristic of the captivity and restoration while conceding it in earlier psalms; Keil and Delitzsch place it as the last of its kind in the collection and describe its strophes changing length partway through.
outliers: Augustine presses the difficulty that everlasting mercy seems to have no object once the judgment has fixed everyone, and resolves it by the endlessness of the blessedness mercy bestows rather than by an endless supply of misery to relieve.

Calvin quotes a long argument that the poetry of most countries comes in time to depend less on exactness of arrangement and more on external contrivance, and that the burden was probably ordained to help the memory of a people at Babylon cut off from public teaching and reduced to passing their religion down orally.

Keil and Delitzsch report a printed Psalter that arranges the whole psalm in two columns, as is done with the song of Moses, and allow that it answers to the structure though neither tradition nor manuscripts support it.
Spurgeon holds that the works are great in wonder even when not great in size, and that the microscope shows as many marvels as the telescope.
themes: a refrain counted twenty-six times
mercy that outlasts the misery it relieves
plural names for a single God
an earth beaten out like a plate of metal
poetry taking on artifice as memory grows harder

10.pericope_label: To him that smote Egypt in their firstborn: to him which divided the Red sea into parts

schools.summary: Henry observes that only the conquering plague is named, makes the sea a miracle of justice as well as mercy since the same water was a lane to Israel and a grave to their pursuers, argues that the miracles proved the commission of Moses and bound the nation to the law, and distinguishes the power that divided the waters from the power that gave the people courage to walk between them; Spurgeon calls judgment God’s strange work yet needful surgery, describes the last plague wounding every household in its tenderest point, and keeps the design of mercy to Israel and through Israel to all the world.

Gill finds both justice and mercy in the smiting of the firstborn, since Egypt had slain the sons of the Lord’s own firstborn, reports and rejects the tradition of twelve separate paths through the sea, keeps the strong east wind and the two walls of water, and reads the deliverance throughout as a figure of redemption, of afflictions safely passed, and of sins cast into the depths never to rise against the pardoned.

Clarke counts the demographic cost of the last plague, a great part of the rising generation cut off and few but old persons and children left remaining, and reports the tradition of twelve paths through the sea as held by many of the fathers as well as by some of the Jews before asking whether it is very likely.

Ellicott states plainly that the refrain sounds harsh to Christian ears after the destruction of the firstborn and after slaughter, and answers that the word rendered mercy means covenant grace, a favour the heathen did not share and one often shown most signally in their destruction; Keil and Delitzsch mark the tenth verse as the hinge where the psalm turns from God the Creator to the God of the history of salvation, and note that the verb for dividing the sea is not the usual one.

debates: Can the refrain be sung over the destruction of the firstborn? Ellicott raises the difficulty in his own person and answers it from the covenant sense of the word for mercy, which excluded the heathen and was sometimes shown most clearly in their ruin; Spurgeon concedes that judgment is a strange work and calls the punishment needful surgery; Henry makes the crossing a miracle of justice as much as of mercy; Gill finds the stroke just because Egypt had killed the sons of the Lord’s firstborn.

Was the sea divided into two parts or twelve? Gill reports the tradition of a path for each tribe from Jarchi, Kimchi and Arama and answers that it has no foundation; Clarke reports the same opinion among the Jews and adds that many of the fathers held it, then asks whether it is very likely; both keep the two walls of water.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch mark the tenth verse as the point where the psalm stops praising the Creator of all things and begins praising the God of the history of salvation, and note in passing that the verb it uses for dividing the sea is not the one the older narratives use.
Clarke measures the last plague demographically, reckoning that a great part of the rising generation was cut off and that few but old persons and children were left remaining.

Gill turns the overthrow in the sea into a double emblem, of the destruction of Satan and his principalities and of the casting of the sins of God’s people into the depths of the sea, never to appear again to their condemnation.
Henry separates the power that divided the waters from the power that gave the people courage to walk between them, calling the second a power over men’s hearts.
themes: a refrain that has to be defended
the same water a lane and a grave
a tradition of twelve paths refused twice
the point where a psalm changes its subject
plagues counted by the households they emptied

16.pericope_label: To him which led his people through the wilderness: to him which smote great kings

schools.summary: Spurgeon argues that God, having led them into the wilderness, was pledged to lead them through it while leaving it as barren as ever, marvels that a vast host with neither roads nor tracks never lost its way, names Moses and Aaron and Jethro and the pillar of cloud as the means, and holds that their conduct tested the mercy most severely but that it bore the strain.

Gill keeps the wilderness plain, a place with no path where the pillar of cloud and fire showed the way, weighs whether the great kings are the thirty-one kings of the land or the two named next and prefers the second because the others were petty kings, and reads the transfer of the land from idol-servers to God’s servants as a reward of grace and not of debt.

Clarke reduces the wilderness to an astonishing miracle of supply, so many hundreds of thousands maintained for forty years in a country totally deprived of all necessaries for the life of man; Wesley notes that the nation is spoken of as one man because its people were united in one body in the worship of God.

Ellicott finds a stray preposition before the first king’s name, so that the line reads literally to Sihon, and judges that the composer set it there inadvertently after beginning so many verses with it, and that the slip was afterwards copied into the parallel verse of the neighbouring psalm.

debates: Which kings are the great kings? Gill sets the thirty-one kings of the land against the two named in the following verses and prefers the two, on the ground that the kings of the land were petty kings while these were greater ones.
outliers: Ellicott treats a preposition standing before the first king’s name as an authorial slip carried over by habit from the preceding verses, and holds that the neighbouring psalm copied the mistake, which makes this psalm the earlier of the two at that point.
Spurgeon draws the pledge out of the leading: because God brought them into the wilderness he was bound to bring them through it, though the wilderness itself was left as barren as he found it.
Clarke states the wilderness as an arithmetical marvel, hundreds of thousands supplied for forty years in a country with nothing in it for the life of man.
Wesley reads the singular servant as the whole nation spoken of as one man, united in one body in the worship of God.
themes: a host too large to be lost
petty kings weighed against great ones
a preposition left standing by habit
a barren country that stays barren
a people counted as a single servant

23.pericope_label: Who remembered us in our low estate: who giveth food to all flesh: O give thanks unto the God of heaven

schools.summary: Henry reads the many national redemptions as types of the redemption of the universal church and insists the Son was sent for us and not for the angels that sinned, calls God a good housekeeper who feeds so large a family, and makes the closing title that of the great benefactor from whom every good gift descends; Spurgeon takes the low estate wholly personally, as bankruptcy and mendicancy at hell’s mouth, holds that the mercy reaches down even to beasts and reptiles, and sets the throne in glory out of reach of foes.

Gill canvasses Egypt, the days of the Judges and the Babylonian captivity as the low estate, reports one interpreter applying it to the captivity of his own day and answers that they are not yet remembered in a gracious way, spreads the giving of food over Jews and Gentiles and good and bad men with spiritual food added, and takes the closing title of the maker and possessor of heaven where the inheritance is reserved.

Clarke settles the low estate on the captivity in Babylon, finds the fitting of food to endlessly diversified natures an overwhelming proof of providence, and reports that three versions add a twenty-seventh verse by repeating the third, which he calls very unnecessary; Wesley explains that the psalmist teaches us to praise God for the feeding of the creatures on their behalf, because those most concerned either cannot or do not perform the duty.

Ellicott replaces redeemed with snatched us from, a verb used of a lion seizing its prey, raises the appearance that the mercy widens to all men at the feeding of all flesh and denies it on the ground that the covenant grace was Israel’s alone, dates the closing title after the exile, and notes without complaint the repetition of the third verse at the end.

debates: Whose low estate does the psalm remember? Gill offers the bondage in Egypt on Jarchi’s authority, the days of the Judges, and the Babylonian captivity on the authority of Aben Ezra and Kimchi, and reports the last applying it to the captivity of his own people in his own time, which Gill answers by saying they are not yet remembered in a gracious way; Clarke settles on Babylon; Henry makes the national deliverances types of the redemption of the church; Spurgeon takes it of personal experience alone.

Does the mercy of the feeding verse extend beyond Israel? Ellicott raises the question and answers no: the wider range is only apparent, for though Israel could think of God feeding all men as the creator of all, the covenant grace was theirs alone. Spurgeon calls it a boundless mercy that knows no limit from the meanness of its object and reaches even to beasts and reptiles; Gill extends it to Jews and Gentiles and to good men and bad; Henry and Clarke treat it as universal providence.

Does the psalm have a twenty-seventh verse? Clarke reports the Vulgate, the Arabic and the Anglo-Saxon adding one by repeating the third verse, and judges the repetition very unnecessary; Ellicott records the same repetition at the end and points the reader to the Prayer Book without objecting to it.
outliers: Ellicott dates the closing title after the exile and explains it by distance from Zion, the faithful being driven, once the visible token of the divine presence was out of reach, to think of their God as one whose mansion is on high.

Wesley justifies a verse about feeding animals in a hymn of praise by making the worshipper praise God on the creatures’ behalf, since those most concerned in the mercy either cannot or do not perform the duty.
Spurgeon holds that if the Lord could have changed towards anyone it would have been towards those who brought themselves low, kept themselves low, and prepared themselves to sink yet lower.
Ellicott substitutes snatched us from for redeemed, the verb being used elsewhere of a lion suddenly seizing his prey.
themes: a low estate claimed by four different centuries
covenant grace held back from the nations it feeds
a verse added by three versions and printed in a prayer book
praise offered on behalf of creatures who cannot offer it
a divine title that only exile made necessary
